item.title: 🔵 Microsoft: Treat AI agents as insider threats
item.description:
Why this matters: Hospitality-system impact — consider guest services, PMS/POS, and property operations.

EVP of Microsoft Security Hayete Gallot writes in a blog post that AI agents operating independently within companies could be a serious security threat. According to Microsoft, today’s most advanced AI models cannot be fully trusted.

Not because they are malicious, but because they are trained to achieve goals and can take unexpected shortcuts to achieve them. For example, bypassing limitations or cooperating with other AI agents in ways that were not intended.

The problem becomes especially serious when companies allow AI agents to access sensitive information, internal tools, and even allow them to make independent decisions.

item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

Attackers are using stolen connection keys exposed in a TeamUpdraft security breach to install malicious plugins on affected WordPress sites and establish persistent access. Sites already compromised may remain at risk even after the exposed credentials are revoked.

The incident exposed potentially sensitive information, including connection keys used by UpdraftCentral, a service that lets administrators manage multiple WordPress sites remotely.

item.title: 🟠 Google, Mozilla revoke eMudhra intermediates after private key compromise
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

Private keys associated with eight intermediate certificate authorities operated by Indian digital trust provider eMudhra have been compromised, potentially allowing attackers to forge trusted certificates and impersonate websites or services, according to Google and Mozilla.

“On 17th October @ 20:06 UTC, Mozilla received a report to certificates@mozilla.org, forwarded by the Chrome Root program, that the private key of 8 eMudhra Intermediate certificates have been compromised,” Dennis Jackson, a member of Mozilla’s engineering team, wrote in a public Mozilla bug report. “An attacker with the private key of any of the compromised intermediate CAs could impersonate any website or service.”

Mozilla independently recovered the keys later that day, confirming that they were vulnerable.

item.title: 🟠 Moving past autonomous exploitation to machine-speed security
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Frontier AI advancements have created a world where exploitation outpaces defense. The average enterprise takes 32 to 43 days to patch, but the mean time to exploit a vulnerability is 10 hours. This asymmetry creates questions around how enterprises can trust autonomous AI to operate ubiquitously across their environments. As I mentioned on the TechCrunch Disrupt stage last week, security at machine speed means AI accelerates the fix as quickly as it does the find. Below is an expanded take of that discussion.

item.title: 🟠 KVM escape exposes broader attack surface in Linux networking
item.description:
Why this matters: Compliance/regulatory signal — determine applicability and required action.

Security researchers have found a critical flaw in the Linux kernel’s networking stack that can let attackers escape a KVM virtual machine and execute code on the host system. The weakness could also potentially let attackers compromise systems running other Linux-based virtualization and sandbox platforms.

Tracked as CVE-2026-99999 and dubbed PwnEscape, the vulnerability was discovered by researchers from AI-powered pentesting startup Pwn.ai during a $1 million challenge to hack Vercel’s sandbox platform, which uses KVM-based Firecracker microVMs. Rather than exploiting a bug in the KVM hypervisor itself, the attack targets the Linux networking code that handles traffic from inside virtual machines. item.title: 🟠 When defrost becomes sabotage: 3 OT lessons from France’s supermarket attack
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

On the night of 11 October, someone remotely put the cold cases of several hundred French supermarkets into defrost. At Intermarché and Netto stores, fridges and freezers warmed to around 50°C and stayed there for about six hours, according to Les Mousquetaires, which expects losses in the tens of millions of euros. By morning, staff were filling skips with meat, frozen goods and vegetables.

Coopérative U counted 80 affected stores out of roughly 2,000. Its chief executive, Dominique Schelcher, told RTL that the cold chain held in most of them. Only a minority reacted too slowly and lost stock, and he credited store staff and refrigeration contractors for the difference. Intermarché said its affected stores had to throw away everything. A second wave followed in the night of 12 to 13 October, this time also reaching stores with Dixell controllers.

item.title: 🔵 OT systems complicate quantum-resistant data protection
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

Quantum-resistant cryptography presents security leaders with various challenges, but CISOs in industries dependent on IoT and operational technology (OT) devices may face a particularly difficult journey to quantum readiness, especially if sensitive information that must remain confidential for years passes through those devices.

A recent report from cybersecurity firm Forescout highlights these challenges in the healthcare industry, where medical histories, diagnostic images, and laboratory results, which retain their sensitivity long after they are created, routinely get transferred between various operational systems.

Attackers who collect encrypted traffic carrying this information today can store it for decryption when sufficiently powerful quantum computers become available, an approach security experts call “harvest now, decrypt later” (HNDL).


Source: CSO Online  |  Severity: FYI  |  Age: 1d

Microsoft and Nvidia are urging enterprises to assess the security of open-weight AI models throughout deployment, warning that changes to model weights and configurations can weaken safeguards even when a model retains its ability to perform assigned tasks.

In a joint paper published last week, the companies identified 30 risk types across five categories and outlined a process for evaluating, mitigating, and monitoring them. The guidance calls for enterprises to verify model provenance, test the configurations they intend to deploy, and reassess risks after material changes.

“Weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk,” the paper said. “Risk depends on the model, use case, deployment, and safeguards.”

item.title: 🟠 ConnectWise backup credentials exposed multiple Microsoft 365 tenants
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

ConnectWise has disabled key cloud services and is investigating unauthorized access to customers’ Microsoft 365 environments after a credential tied to its Cloud Backup platform was compromised and used to authenticate into customer tenants, prompting Huntress to identify suspicious sign-ins across 162 organizations.

The activity involved the Cloud Backup application obtaining Microsoft Graph access tokens using a credential associated with ConnectWise’s own tenant. Security firm Huntress has also confirmed unauthorized sign-ins across 162 tenants as of 19:00 UTC on October 16.

Huntress said the application authenticated from the IP address 144.172.64[.]128 on October 15, between 06.13 and 08.34 UTC. The address belonged to a hosting provider, rather than the Azure private IP space from which the application normally communicated. The authentication events were recorded in Microsoft’s sign-in logs.

item.title: 🔵 The password nobody owns: Taking machines to zero standing privilege (ZSP)
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Ask your infrastructure lead who owns the service account behind the overnight finance batch and notice how long the answer takes. In many of the environments I’ve reviewed, the engineer who set it up left years ago and the password has been sitting in a vault, or sometimes a plain config file, ever since. It usually still carries permissions sized for a migration that wrapped up before anyone on the current team joined, so people leave it alone rather than risk breaking something nobody fully understands.

Multiply that across the landscape, and the numbers get uncomfortable quickly. Palo Alto Networks surveyed more than 2,900 security leaders for its 2026 Identity Security Landscape and found an average of 109 machine identities for every human one.

item.title: 🔴 Hallucinated domain in official OpenAI skill underscores AI supply chain risks
item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

Researchers have discovered a first-of-its-kind supply-chain vulnerability in OpenAI’s official skills repository.

OpenAI maintains an official GitHub repository of skills that teach AI agents how to work with various platforms and services. As an official skill, these components are often given an implicit level of trust because they are contributed or vetted by verified vendors.

Snags arose because one OpenAI skill — designed to teach agents the best way to deploy applications on Render — instructed production apps to send their tokens to an unregistered domain (render-internal.com).

Discovering this flaw, researchers from AIR Security’s Research Lab registered the domain and pointed it at a passive (listening-only) sinkhole, which started receiving tokens and API calls from real production apps.

Testing the skill with Codex confirmed that the domain made its way into real application code as the default option.

item.title: 🟠 Linux kernel gets a fix for a flaw that enabled attackers to escape VMs
item.description:
Why this matters: Compliance/regulatory signal — determine applicability and required action.

The Linux kernel’s networking stack was found vulnerable to a guest-to-host escape attack, in which an attacker operating inside a virtual machine (VM) could cross the isolation boundary and access the underlying host.

Dubbed PwnEscape and tracked as CVE-2026-99999, a flaw allowed guest-controlled packet metadata to trigger a write that changes an IPv4 header after the kernel has already processed it. That flaw could be chained with additional exploitation techniques to achieve host-level code execution.

The problem was discovered by security researcher Paulos Yibelo of Pwn.ai while participating in Vercel’s $1 million Sandbox security challenge, announced on August 18. The challenge invited researchers to test the isolation boundaries of Vercel’s sandboxing infrastructure, including whether they could escape the virtual machine itself and reach the host.

item.description:

Organizations running self-hosted BeyondTrust Remote Support should treat exposed appliances as potentially compromised after a suspected Chinese espionage group exploited a critical zero-day to gain root control, access credential vaults, and establish footholds for lateral movement, according to Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group.

“Organizations should prepare for potential widespread exploitation following this disclosure,” Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant said in a blog post. The post attributes the zero-day exploitation to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor formerly tracked as UNC5221, and dates it to late August.
